key_insight: Machine-learned simulations show that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far more slowly than in bulk because surface pathways are constrained and vacancies trap electrons nearby.
engineering_relevance: The results explain why porous rutile TiO2 can exhibit much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, informing surface engineering for catalysis, photovoltaics, and energy-storage devices.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to a redox-active oxide surface.
Ran nanosecond-scale finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Analyzed polaron hopping pathways, vacancy effects, and free-energy landscapes.
evidence_signal: The study uses several nanoseconds of simulated dynamics across multiple temperatures to quantify polaron mobility and hopping statistics beyond the reach of standard ab initio molecular dynamics.
watch_item: The approach is demonstrated on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110), so transferability to other oxides and surface terminations should be validated case by case.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
